drills.title: Postulating implication introduction
hints: Postulate, without proof, `implies_intro`: for propositions p and q given as parameters, a function from Proof p to Proof q yields a Proof of Implies p q.

drills.title: Proving p → q → p
hints: Declare p as an implicit variable of type Prop, and then, separately, q likewise.
Theorem `t1`: p → q → p, proved by a lambda taking hp : p, whose body is a lambda taking hq : q, returning hp; annotate both binders.

drills.title: Printing a proof term
hints: Theorem `t1`: p → q → p, proved by a lambda taking hp : p, whose body is a lambda taking hq : q, returning hp; annotate both binders.
Print the proof of t1.

drills.title: Quantifying over propositions explicitly
hints: Theorem `t1`: for all propositions p and q, quantified implicitly in the statement itself, p → q → p.
Prove it with a single lambda that binds p and q implicitly (with their type), then hp : p and hq : q, and returns hp.

drills.title: Disjunction is commutative
hints: Declare variables p, q, r of type Prop.
An anonymous example: from `h : p ∨ q`, prove q ∨ p, as a term.
Eliminate h with Or.elim: in the first case, given hp, inject it on the right with Or.inr; in the second, given hq, inject it on the left with Or.inl. Leave the lambda binders unannotated.

drills.title: Anything follows from a contradiction
hints: Declare variables p and q of type Prop.
An anonymous example: from `hp : p` and `hnp : ¬p`, prove q, by False.elim applied to the result of applying hnp to hp.

drills.title: Swapping a conjunction, both ways
hints: Declare variables p and q of type Prop.
Theorem `and_swap`: p ∧ q ↔ q ∧ p, proved by building the iff directly from its two directions with the anonymous constructor.
Each direction is the same: a lambda over h that builds a pair from h's right component and h's left component, accessed by field projection.
An anonymous example: from `h : p ∧ q`, prove q ∧ p by applying the forward direction (mp) of and_swap, instantiated at p and q, to h.

drills.title: Double negation by cases
hints: Open the Classical namespace.
Declare a variable p of type Prop.
An anonymous example: from `h : ¬¬p`, prove p, by byCases on p.
In the case where p holds, a lambda over an annotated h1 : p simply returns it.
In the case where ¬p holds, a lambda over an annotated h1 : ¬p derives the goal by absurd from h1 and h.

drills.title: Double negation by contradiction
hints: Open the Classical namespace.
Declare a variable p of type Prop.
An anonymous example: from `h : ¬¬p`, prove p, by byContradiction.
Its argument is a lambda over an annotated h1 : ¬p, whose body explicitly states that it proves False, justified by applying h to h1.
